newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Hindu party slips in bid for power.
newsitem.headline: India's Hindu party slips in bid for power.

text.p: The Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), riven by internal dissent and failure to clinch a majority in India's most populous state, has slipped in its drive for national power, analysts and politicans say.
Its latest setback, after briefly tasting national power in May, was in northern Uttar Pradesh state, where it failed to win an outright majority in local polls that ended last week.
Other problems since June have included a split in the right-wing BJP's ranks in the western state of Gujarat and corruption charges against some of its leaders.
"It is no longer a credible claimant to the throne in New Delhi. It certainly needs to do some soul-searching," analyst Pran Chopra, with the independent Centre for Policy Research, said on Sunday.
Rasheed Talib, an independent political commentator, said: "These trends undermine the strength and performance of the party.
"They have diluted their identity," he said, adding the BJP now was being seen by many voters as just one among many other political parties in the world's largest democracy.
The BJP emerged as the single largest party, with 160 deputies in the 545-seat national parliament, after inconclusive general elections in April and May.
The BJP formed a minority government in May but it lasted only 12 days before Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda cobbled together a centre-left coalition, the United Front (UF).
The BJP built its national foundation on a Hindu revivalist agenda in Uttar Pradesh in the late 1980s.
It had hoped to win control of the state -- mainly Hindu India's biggest state electoral prize.
It won the most seats, 177, in the state with 140 million people but was short of a majority in the 425-member assembly. The UF was second with 134 seats.
"It is undoubtedly a disappointment against the expectations," Jaswant Singh, a BJP leader, told Reuters.
In Gujarat, the BJP government was dislodged by New Delhi after its state party split and a breakaway faction formed a separate regional party.
"As far as Gujarat is concerned, it was not a happy experience. It was a setback," Singh said.
There have been murmurs of dissent in other regional party outfits, which BJP officials call growth pangs.
Analysts said the BJP had been forced to grope for issues, particularly after the dilution of its Hindu revivalist agenda.
Its image suffered when Hindu fanatics tore down the 16th century Babri Mosque in the northern town of Ayodhya in 1992, sparking nationwide riots in which around 3,000 people died.
Fearing a backlash, the BJP moved to distance itself from militant Hindu groups.
The BJP's rivals call it "communal" because they claim it alienates minority Moslems. About 120 million of India's estimated 950 million people are Moslem.
Militant Hindu groups have staked their claim to two more mosques in Uttar Pradesh, saying they stood on temple structures. But BJP has distanced itself from these groups.
"The party's once reliable fallback, Ayodhya, has run its course and seems unlikely to lend itself to revival," the Times of India newspaper said on Sunday.
The BJP, the first to raise the idea of economic liberalisation, was robbed of this agenda when the former Congress government launched wide-ranging reforms in 1992.
Analysts said the BJP was going through a transition, marked by changes in Indian society, and was in the process of searching for new political and social alliances.
"I see BJP emerging as the right of the centre focal point," Talib said.
